article.articleSummary:

A July 12 government report, with data through July 10, shows the outbreak expanding to five provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Chopo. Haut-Uele and Chopo are newly included in the national outbreak map; infections in these areas are linked to the Ituri cluster. Transmission is attributed to population movements and refugee displacement from Ituri. Currently, 763 confirmed cases are isolated or receiving hospital care. National hospital bed occupancy stands at 95.1%. Recoveries total 306, while 299 cases are still classified as suspected. The report signals ongoing, multi-province transmission driven by mobility, with the outbreak intensifying in new areas.

article.articleSummary: Viral encephalitis is a dangerous brain infection; about 70% of cases have a viral etiology. It splits into primary viral encephalitis, where viruses directly invade the CNS, and secondary encephalitis, a complication after measles, mumps, or influenza. Japanese encephalitis virus, Herpes Simplex virus, and Epstein–Barr virus are common culprits; Enterovirus causes cases in children. Japanese encephalitis outbreaks typically occur May–July, mainly in children aged 2–8, transmitted by mosquitoes; Enterovirus encephalitis often affects children under 5 from March–June via the digestive route; HSV encephalitis can occur year‑round in both children and adults. Most viral encephalitis lacks specific antiviral therapy, except HSV encephalitis, which can be treated early with antivirals. Management is largely supportive in neurology/ICU settings, to control brain edema, seizures, fever, and vital functions; vaccination is advised for Japanese encephalitis, and mosquito control and hygiene reduce risk. article.articleHeadline: Facing Typhoon Bavi: Emergency relief continue as health risks emerge
article.articleSummary: Following Typhoon Bavi, heavy rainfall, flooding and standing water raise post-typhoon health risks, per the regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Water- and food-borne diseases may rise as floods damage water supply and sewage networks, and foods exposed to floodwater pose risks. Residents should drink bottled, boiled or otherwise safe water and avoid cloudy or odorous tap water; emphasize frequent handwashing with soap, sanitation, and regular cleaning to reduce intestinal infections. Mosquito- and rodent-borne diseases are heightened by stagnant water and waste, increasing the risk of dengue fever and chikungunya. Remove standing water around homes, balconies, rooftops, basements and green spaces; dispose of garbage promptly; store food in sealed containers. Avoid walking barefoot in floodwater or handling contaminated water and waste with bare hands. If rodent signs appear, do not touch droppings; wear gloves and masks during cleanup and disinfect affected areas before disposal.

article.articleHeadline: Penza residents were reminded of what diseases can be contracted from a mosquito bite.
article.articleSummary: West Nile fever, a mosquito-borne disease highlighted by Rospotrebnadzor, was first identified in Russia in 1999 and remains endemic in the southern regions. The virus is not transmitted between people. Prevention centers on reducing bites: use repellents outdoors, install window screens, and employ insect-killing devices; eliminate standing water on private plots, balconies, and loggias; wear clothing that fully covers the body when in parks or near water. Travelers to tropical climates should follow the same precautions and check with tour operators about regional outbreak status. Symptoms include high fever, headache, muscle pains, and a skin rash; seek urgent medical care if these appear. West Nile fever is found in warm climates, including Egypt, Greece, Israel, Thailand, Vietnam, India, and many regions across Africa, Asia, Europe, and North America.

article.articleHeadline: Next two weeks critical as dengue risk soars
article.articleSummary: Dengue risk in Sri Lanka's Western Province is extremely high over the next two weeks as mosquito larvae density rises, with 66,064 dengue cases and 46 deaths recorded this year. July alone saw 10,685 cases, including 1,030 yesterday, and the Western Province accounts for 52.7% of total cases, with Gampaha District now the hotspot ahead of Colombo. Hospitals in the Western Province are overwhelmed, some beds housing two to three patients. Early outbreak signals appeared in December–January; the Southwest Monsoon (May–July) typically elevates transmission, while the February–April heat reduced breeding. Three dengue vaccines are approved abroad and used in Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia; Sri Lanka would evaluate a two-dose regimen, noting delayed immunity and strong effectiveness mainly for those previously infected. Special dengue-control operations, involving armed forces, are underway nationwide.

The article notes a potential future funding decline, with MSF France’s Stéphane Doyon explaining that most malaria treatments arriving in centers outside MSF-provisioned facilities are funded by the Global Fund, and without it those treatments may not arrive. North Kivu is described as one of the province’s most critical health areas amid a humanitarian crisis and procurement challenges. Malaria remains the leading cause of consultations in MSF centers. The region is also experiencing outbreaks of measles and cholera, with a population traumatized by war and requiring external support to sustain essential health services.

article.articleHeadline: A patient suspected of having the Ebola virus was placed in a hotel in Equatorial Guinea with deportees from the United States, according to lawyers.
article.articleSummary: Equatorial Guinea's Bioko Island hotel in Malabo, owned by President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, is used as a detention site for migrants under a third-country deportation deal with the United States. Reports indicate a man suspected of Ebola was transported to the facility by medical staff in full PPE and isolated on a lower floor; a woman was reportedly placed in isolation as well. The facility currently houses 4 women and 13 men, all with U.S. court orders meant to shield them from deportation. The hotel, previously a COVID-19 isolation site, reportedly lacks adequate PPE, sanitation, or medical care for seriously ill detainees. Ebola outbreaks are ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with over 600 deaths since May, and Uganda has confirmed cases; Equatorial Guinea has not reported any Ebola cases and is distant from Congo. A US-backed deal near $7.5 million transformed the hotel into a detention center, with eight African countries having similar arrangements.

The City Health Services Office, in coordination with hospitals, is closely monitoring cases and enforcing measures to prevent transmission within health facilities. Authorities urge continued vigilance and stronger infection-prevention protocols in hospitals, while residents are advised to follow basic precautions: wear masks in crowded areas, wash hands regularly, and stay home when ill. article.articleHeadline: High-risk patients lack awareness of shingles prevention; organization urges the government to subsidize vaccines.
article.articleSummary: Shingles prevention awareness is low among Hong Kong’s high‑risk patients, prompting calls for government vaccine subsidies. A March survey by Seven Major Patient Organizations found about 30% of respondents experienced two or more recurrences, and 20% required hospitalization; postherpetic neuralgia and emotional distress were common. High‑risk patients use emergency and hospital services more often, with average outpatient costs around HK$2,425 and inpatient costs between HK$22,700 and HK$38,300 per admission, underscoring the health and economic burden. Advocates urge embedding preventive care in disease‑management reform and public‑health financing, with vaccine subsidies initially covering immunocompromised groups such as rheumatic disease patients and organ transplant recipients, then expanding to other chronic diseases. Experts warn of severe complications—ophthalmic zoster, facial palsy, stroke, acute viral encephalitis, and pneumonia—that are more likely and serious in immunocompromised individuals."

article.articleHeadline: Nanning carries out comprehensive disinfection across disaster-affected areas; technology supports post-disaster epidemic prevention.
article.articleSummary: After Typhoon Meishak caused heavy rainfall and severe floods in Hengzhou City and Binyang County, Guangxi, Nanning launched comprehensive post-disaster epidemic prevention. A 500-plus professional disinfection team, employing drones and manual disinfection with smart coverage, targeted Yunbao (Yunbiao) Town, Xiaoyi Town, and Gantang Town in disaster zones. The Nanning Health Commission deployed 20 CDC technicians to relief sites and emergency clinics to quickly conduct epidemiological investigations and sampling for diarrheal symptoms and other key illnesses. More than 50 water samples from factory and tap water were collected for quality monitoring, with corrective actions issued for any unqualified results to ensure drinking-water safety. Going forward, the health system will continue full-area environmental disinfection, guide the restart and retesting of water plants, and strengthen routine infectious disease surveillance to safeguard residents’ health in the disaster-affected areas.

article.articleHeadline: A tiny insect bite nearly cost an elderly woman her life; if you suspect scrub typhus, please seek medical attention promptly.
article.articleSummary: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) caused a near-fatal multi-organ failure in a 70-year-old woman in Xiamen, Fujian Province, China. After a chigger bite during outdoor work, she developed a sustained fever up to 41°C and rapidly progressed to respiratory, circulatory, renal, hepatic, and coagulation failure, requiring ICU care at Xiamen University Affiliated Haicang Hospital for about two weeks before recovery and discharge. Chiggers inhabit grasses, shrubs, and forested areas; bites are painless due to anesthetic saliva, often leading to delayed diagnosis. The report urges that after outdoor activity, persistent high fever with a painless eschar, along with body aches, fatigue, or rash, warrants prompt medical attention and disclosure of outdoor exposure. Early diagnosis and treatment can reduce fever within 1–3 days and achieve a high cure rate.

article.articleSummary: COVID-19 death in Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh, India: a 46-year-old man died after four days of heavy antibiotics with little improvement, highlighting that the threat persists as cases re-emerge. SARS-CoV-2 spreads mainly via airborne particles, especially in poorly ventilated spaces. Incubation is 2–14 days. Symptoms include loss of taste and smell, shortness of breath, cold/flu‑like symptoms, and diarrhea; emergency signs include severe breathing difficulty, skin, lips or nails turning yellow, gray, or blue, sudden confusion, or chest pain. Prevention hinges on vaccination, particularly updated vaccines for those over 65, the immunocompromised, pregnant women, and people with heart or lung disease or obesity. Other measures: avoid contact with sick individuals, wash hands for at least 20 seconds, disinfect surfaces, avoid crowded, poorly ventilated places, and wear a mask in such settings. If positive or exposed, consult a healthcare professional; high-risk patients may receive therapies that limit viral spread. Source: Mayo Clinic.

article.articleHeadline: How to keep skin safe during the monsoon? NMCH experts have answered every question; these mistakes can be costly - Monsoon skincare: NMCH expert tips to prevent fungal infections.
article.articleSummary: Patna-based NMCH dermatologist Dr. Vikas Shankar advised during Hello Jagran that monsoon humidity boosts fungal infections and skin issues such as tinea (ringworm) in folds of skin, between toes, thighs, underarms, and neck, along with dermatitis, eczema, and acne. Prevention centers on daily bathing, thorough drying, and immediately changing wet clothes; wear breathable cotton and loose clothing. Use sunscreen as needed due to UV exposure even in rainy weather. Do not apply steroid creams or medications without a doctor’s guidance, as they can worsen infections. Seek dermatological care for persistent itching, red patches, blisters, or color changes; maintain hydration and balanced diet to help acne. For children with prickly heat, keep skin dry in cotton clothing. If the whole family experiences itching, consider scabies and ensure collective treatment. Melasma or dark spots require sun protection and medical advice. Daily skincare and professional guidance are key to preventing complications.

article.articleHeadline: He discovered a one-meter-long tapeworm after traveling to India, and three years later doctors found 38 parasites in his brain: "I never thought something like this could happen to me."
article.articleSummary: Neurocysticercosis caused by Taenia solium infection led to 38 cerebral cysts in a British woman after traveling to India in 2007. Three years after returning, she expelled a roughly one-meter tapeworm, prompting medical review. About a year later she developed severe headaches and a first seizure; brain imaging revealed 38 parasites lodged in the brain. Initial suspicion of toxoplasmosis was ruled out; diagnosis confirmed as neurocysticercosis, a rare brain infection in the United Kingdom. She received antiparasitic therapy and corticosteroids, achieving initial control, but years later experienced a relapse with severe brain inflammation, paranoia and psychosis, necessitating six months in a neuropsychiatric unit. Over time the parasites died and calcified, avoiding surgery. She has not had seizures since 2017 but remains on lifelong anti-epileptic medication. She now advocates awareness to this rare, potentially grave disease.

article.articleHeadline: Chandipura Virus Symptoms: Fever, headache, vomiting, seizures to death!... In the monsoon season in Gujarat, a virus infection is spreading to children's brains via flies... What are the symptoms of this deadly disease? Learn tips to survive.
article.articleSummary: As of July 12, 2026, in Gujarat during the monsoon season, Chandipura virus—a vector-borne infection transmitted mainly by Phlebotomus sand flies—has been linked to brain infections in children. The disease primarily affects children under 15 and can cause severe encephalitis with rapid neurological deterioration, presenting with fever, headache, vomiting, and seizures; outcomes may be fatal. There is currently no specific vaccine or antiviral therapy for Chandipura virus; management relies on supportive medical care and addressing complications. Transmission occurs through bites of Phlebotomus sand flies, highlighting vector control and protection against flies as key public health measures. The article emphasizes the seriousness of the situation in Gujarat's monsoon season and underscores the lack of targeted pharmacological treatments, necessitating vigilant clinical management and vector prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Hepatitis-A outbreak in Kaithal puts Haryanas Health Dept on alert - The Tribune
article.articleSummary: Hepatitis-A outbreak in Kaithal, Haryana, centered on Sajuma village in Kalayat block, has prompted a high-alert response. A door-to-door survey of 1,477 residents identified suspected cases and abdominal-pain complaints; 37 blood samples were tested for Hepatitis-A, Hepatitis-E, and liver function. Twenty-three were confirmed positive for Hepatitis-A; no Hepatitis-E cases detected so far; final PGI report awaited. One death has been reported, not yet officially linked to Hepatitis-A. Three patients are hospitalized (one government, two private) and stable. The Health Department deployed round-the-clock medical teams and ambulance services in the village. Preventive measures include distribution of 10,143 halogen tablets, 200 ORS packets, and zinc tablets, plus hygiene and sanitation awareness campaigns. Residents are advised to drink boiled or properly treated water and report jaundice symptoms promptly; rumours should be ignored. As of 12 July 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue outbreak on the rise in Dhanbad; doctors also infected; isolation ward not prepared at SNMMCH.
article.articleSummary: Dengue outbreak rises in Dhanbad, Jharkhand, as of July 2026, with one patient hospitalized at SNMMCH and two doctors infected (both stable). The 32-year-old Santosh Kumar, resident of Bartand, is receiving treatment; a medical team will assess him Monday. Senior physician Dr. Anita Chaudhary of Sadar Hospital and in-charge of Sadar PHC also tested positive. Container surveys identified 22 sites with considerable dengue larvae, prompting removal of stagnant water and vessels’ contents, with planned bleaching sprays and public awareness campaigns. SNMMCH lacks a prepared isolation ward, so dengue patients are housed with general patients; testing is arranged at SNMMCH and Sadar Hospital. Highly susceptible areas include Jharia, Sijua, Dhansar, and Katras, with Sijua experiencing dengue annually. Emphasis remains on sanitation, avoiding standing water, and timely reporting to authorities.

article.articleHeadline: Rising outbreak of lumpy skin disease among animals in Jalalgarh, farmers' concerns rise.
article.articleSummary: Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) is spreading among animals in Jalalgarh block, causing rising concerns among livestock owners. According to veterinarians, cases are reported across almost all panchayats in Jalalgarh, with newborn calves and weaker animals most affected. Many farmers misinterpret LSD as ordinary cowpox, delaying treatment and worsening outcomes, including fatalities in some cases. LSD is a contagious viral disease that spreads through contact with infected animals and via vectors such as flies, mosquitoes, and other insects. Affected animals develop nodules on the body, high fever, reduced appetite, and a drop in milk production, with severe illness possible if not treated promptly. Dr. Aditya Kumar cautions farmers to promptly treat symptomatic animals and consult veterinarians, and to isolate affected stock in clean, safe enclosures to curb transmission.

article.articleHeadline: SoBo tops dengue, malaria charts
article.articleSummary: South Mumbai emerged as the city’s worst-hit mosquito-borne zone in June. D Ward (Malabar Hill, Walkeshwar, Cumballa Hill, Tardeo, Grant Road, Girgaon) recorded the most dengue cases (15), while E Ward (Byculla, Mazgaon, Nagpada, Agripada, Mumbai Central) reported the highest malaria burden (64). A Ward had no confirmed dengue (three suspected). Breeding-site data mirrored disease burden: Anopheles (malaria) sites in E Ward numbered 722, while E Ward also had the most Aedes sites (1,237); yet D Ward saw the most dengue, underscoring that mosquito density alone does not dictate transmission. BMC has intensified anti-larval measures, source reduction, fogging and inspections amid heavy rainfall. Ward teams focus on residential, construction and commercial sites to detect clusters. E Ward also reported 34 acute gastroenteritis and 9 typhoid cases; hepatitis and leptospirosis were not significantly increased.

article.articleHeadline: The hunt for hidden TB: How AI is changing India's fight against tuberculosis
article.articleSummary: VMTB and CATB, two AI tools from Wadhwani AI, advance India's TB control. VMTB uses AI-driven geospatial analytics to predict high-TB-risk areas, integrating TB data with over 20 indicators (population density, air quality, proximity to facilities) on a 500×500-metre grid to generate localized vulnerability rankings for villages and urban wards, guiding targeted active case finding and micro-planning. Integrated with the Ni-kshay portal, Haryana and Assam show improved TB detection. CATB, an offline Android app, analyzes cough sounds and symptoms to screen for presumptive pulmonary TB; after consent and registration, three coughs are recorded and analyzed, with presumptive cases referred for confirmatory tests and Ni-kshay updates. Deployed in 17 states and 148 districts, CATB has screened over 175,000 people aged 7–100, with 12–16% of detected TB cases being asymptomatic. As of 13 July 2026, the approach emphasizes proactive identification to curb transmission.

article.articleHeadline: The Effects of Deforestation Force Forest Mosquitoes to Change Their Feeding Preferences and Bite Humans
article.articleSummary: Deforestation in Brazil's Atlantic Forest (as of July 12, 2026) forces wild mosquitoes to shift feeding toward humans. In two protected areas ringed by settlements in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, now reduced to about one-third of its original extent, researchers from Oswaldo Cruz Institute and the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro captured 1,714 female mosquitoes across 52 species using light traps. DNA analysis of blood meals revealed that 18 of 24 accurately identified samples contained human blood, with others showing dog, rat, bird, and amphibian blood; one specimen carried a mixed amphibian-human blood meal, illustrating flexible host choice. Forest mosquitoes, vectors of yellow fever, Zika, dengue, chikungunya, and Mayaro, thus raise spillover risk as humans near forests become frontline exposure. Habitat loss from human activity accelerates this risk. The findings underscore that ecosystem balance acts as a shield against future outbreaks.

article.articleHeadline: Monsoon is here and so are the mosquitoes
article.articleSummary: Masses of monsoon mosquitoes drive dengue, malaria, and chikungunya risk across India, with Delhi-based National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control noting 121,824 dengue cases and 100+ deaths in 2025. Three core genetic strategies—Sterile Insect Techniques (SIT), Wolbachia Bacterial Modification (WBM), and Gene Drives (CRISPR-Cas9)—have been deployed to suppress or replace wild mosquitoes in various countries. The United States has allowed localized GMO releases; Brazil conducted wide SIT and WBM releases in urban dengue hotspots; Africa, Australia, and Southeast Asia have run similar programs. Evolutionary resistance and regulatory/ethical hurdles limit effectiveness, with engineered mosquitoes often having lower fitness requiring massive, ongoing releases. The article argues for reduced breeding and early diagnosis, plus lightweight, practical measures (well-lit, dry spaces, white/light walls, screens, and covered water storage) to curb transmission. A world without mosquitoes would prevent over seven lakh deaths annually but disrupt ecosystems.

article.articleHeadline: Monoclonal antibodies, cancer's nemesis, will cure dengue too! For the first time in the world, such a treatment is coming to this country.
article.articleSummary: Monoclonal antibodies, a cancer therapy concept, are being developed as a dengue treatment by Serum Institute of India. The lab-made antibody therapy aims to neutralize dengue virus via injections, offering a targeted approach that destroys infected cells with minimal pain. A third-phase clinical trial is currently under way in the country, with plans to extend trials next year to Brazil, Malaysia, and Thailand. The therapy targets all four dengue virus serotypes (DEN-1 to DEN-4). Monoclonal antibodies are produced in laboratories and administered to bolster the body’s defense against the virus. Dengue is noted to be evolving, with reports of more severe symptoms such as abdominal infection, muscle cramps, brain hemorrhage, and retinal damage, per studies cited by the National Institute of Health. No definitive dengue cure exists yet, and a dengue vaccine remains in research.

article.articleHeadline: Company must compensate for COVID-19 infection.
article.articleSummary: Published 2026-07-12, Brazil’s Superior Labor Court (TST), Second Panel, held that a transport company must compensate a long-haul truck driver who contracted COVID-19 on a service trip, recognizing a presumption of causal link due to elevated exposure risk. The worker, hired in 2017, alleged he was not removed from duties during the pandemic and lacked adequate PPE. In November 2020, on a 40+ hour trip, he developed symptoms and was treated in Mossoró, Rio Grande do Norte. In Ceará he developed fever, headaches, body pain, and anosmia, was admitted to ICU, and discharged in February 2021 with sequelae including hearing loss, pressure ulcers, leg pain and numbness, plus psychological injuries. Logs showed more than a month on the road away from the company base. The TRT had questioned the link, but Justice Delaíde Miranda Arantes affirmed elevated trucking risk, shifted the burden to prove non-work infection to the employer, and, unanimously, reinstated damages: moral R$38,000 and aesthetic R$29,000.

article.articleHeadline: Acre has one of the highest tuberculosis case incidence rates in Brazil | ContilNet Notícias
article.articleSummary: TB in Acre, Brazil: Acre shows 56.8 TB incidence per 100,000 in 2025, with 502 new cases, placing it among seven states with rates above 50 per 100k. The Epidemiological Bulletin updated June 2026 by Brazil's Ministry of Health notes Acre's relatively high incidence but favorable clinical management, including one of the highest cure proportions for new lab-confirmed TB cases. In 2024, Acre achieved an 83.2% cure rate, well above the national average of 65.5%. Other states with high cure rates include Amapá 78.5% (n=245), Rio de Janeiro 72.4% (n=6,502), Roraima 70.7% (n=248), Tocantins 69.9% (n=93). Nationally, rapid molecular testing for TB (TRM-TB) tests increased 76.3% between 2021 and 2025, improving early detection. TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, mainly pulmonary, transmitted via airborne routes; diagnosis uses TRM-TB, smear, culture, drug susceptibility testing, and chest X-ray as a supplementary tool. Vulnerable groups include people deprived of liberty, elderly, and children/adolescents.

article.articleHeadline: The First Fleet, the Beginning of British Colonization in Oceania, Could Have Unleashed a Historical Tragedy: Smallpox Would Have Left Millions of Victims in Australia.
article.articleSummary: Smallpox linked to British colonization of Australia caused a devastating potential epidemic. In April 1789, about 16 months after the First Fleet's arrival, smallpox killed Aboriginal people around Sydney. A Nature Human Behaviour study using transmission models traces the outbreak to the British settlement, estimating the disease could have spread over 21 years, reaching miles away, and causing up to 220,000 deaths. The voyage's length may have functioned as quarantine; no virulent outbreak is recorded on board. The virus could have been carried in variola material aboard surgeons' supplies from Britain or during stops in Rio de Janeiro or Cape Town. Other researchers estimate pre-1788 Aboriginal population at 2.51 million, with up to 2.39 million additional deaths by 1861 due to disease, hunger, land loss, displacement, and frontier violence. Alternative northern route via Makassan fishermen from Indonesia is unlikely. WHO eradicated smallpox in 1980; the colonial project inflicted enduring harm.

article.articleHeadline: Girl from Pio IX dies in Picos, and the case is under investigation for suspected severe dengue.

The ultimate cause of death awaits Lacen's laboratory results; no release date for the analyses has been provided.

article.articleHeadline: Venezuela shifts from searching for earthquake victims to disease prevention and control.

In La Guaira, the Brazilian army has established a field hospital, with the Brazilian Navy medical team providing emergency care and treating about 1,400 patients to date. Health burdens are increasingly infectious disease–related as systems remain overwhelmed. The World Health Organization warns of a serious outbreak risk for yellow fever, dengue fever, and malaria. The official death toll from the two earthquakes has risen to 4,118. Emphasis is on infection control, vaccination and vector control, and expanding medical capacity to prevent cascading outbreaks while relief and reconstruction continue.

article.articleHeadline: Carandaí Guides Students on Neglected Diseases and COVID-19 Prevention.
article.articleSummary: Carandaí, Brazil, hosted school-based health education on neglected diseases and COVID-19 prevention for students from Antônio Vicente Barbosa and Municipal Maximiano Ramos Filho. The program covered tuberculosis, leprosy, Chagas disease, schistosomiasis, and leishmaniasis, detailing disease characteristics, symptoms, transmission, prevention, and treatment, with emphasis on early diagnosis to initiate care and monitor progression. Prevention guidance focused on practical daily measures to reduce transmission and protect health within classrooms and families. The COVID-19 component reinforced individual and collective protections to minimize exposure in school and community life. The effort, supported by Carandaí City Hall, integrates health promotion with education to empower children and adolescents and extend information to their communities.

article.articleHeadline: Recife records 2,600 cases of viral hepatitis in ten years and launches a prevention campaign.
article.articleSummary: Recife, Brazil, recorded 2,647 viral hepatitis cases from 2015–2025: 1,342 Hepatitis C (50.7%), 1,208 Hepatitis B (45.6%), and 97 Hepatitis A (3.7%). The burden disproportionately affects older adults: 60.2% of Hepatitis C infections and 36.7% of Hepatitis B infections occur in people aged 50+ or elderly. In response, the Recife City Health Department launched Julho Amarelo (Yellow July) to raise awareness, prevention, and control of viral hepatitis, prioritizing seniors due to rising vulnerability to sexually transmitted infections. Activities include health education, rapid testing for Hep B and C, vaccination, condom distribution, and prevention guidance at health units and community centers during July. A new Hepatitis reference service will open July 23 at SAE Josefa Severina Conceição, within Policlínica Albert Sabin. Early diagnosis and treatment reduce transmission and prevent progression to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

article.articleHeadline: Três Lagoas City Hall confirms third case of meningococcal meningitis in the city.
article.articleSummary: Three cases of meningococcal meningitis have been confirmed in Três Lagoas, Brazil, with the third case announced on Saturday, July 11, 2026. The infection is caused by Neisseria meningitidis and spreads person-to-person via saliva droplets and respiratory secretions. The first case was serogroup B, while the second and third were serogroup C. The patient is hospitalized and under medical care. The Municipal Health Secretariat and Epidemiological Surveillance have launched investigations, identified and monitored close contacts, and implemented prevention and control measures per national protocols. Meningococcal meningitis is a notifiable disease, enabling rapid investigation to reduce transmission and allow timely controls. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, and rash. Vaccination remains the primary prevention, offered free by SUS per the National Vaccination Schedule; vaccination status should be up to date, and close contacts may receive preventive antibiotics.

article.articleHeadline: Sesapi foresees new high-complexity healthcare services and reinforces dengue alert.
article.articleSummary: State health department Sesapi in Piauí, Brazil, outlines a second-half 2026 expansion of high-complexity healthcare in the interior, installing hemodynamics equipment in Floriano and Picos; adding magnetic resonance imaging services in Floriano and Parnaíba; and introducing oncology services in Picos, Parnaíba, and Floriano. The aim is to decentralize access to advanced care and reduce patient travel to Teresina, with multiple deployments scheduled for the semester. In parallel, Sesapi reinforces dengue vigilance ahead of the rainy season, training and guiding municipalities to strengthen prevention and outbreak response. Officials warn dengue transmission is expected to increase toward year's end with the rainy period, and emphasize ongoing capacity-building and dissemination of knowledge to minimize dengue incidences. Quotation from Secretary Dirceu Campêlo underscores the schedule of critical deliveries and decentralization.

article.articleHeadline: Bulletin points to a decline in dengue and chikungunya cases in Cuiabá in 2026.
article.articleSummary: Cuiabá, Brazil — Epidemiological Bulletin No. 24/2026 shows a decline in dengue and chikungunya in 2026. In the 25th Epidemiological Week, 9 dengue and 3 chikungunya cases were notified. Year-to-date weekly averages: dengue down from 75.6 to 51.8; chikungunya down from 434.9 to 4.8. By July 2, 2026, dengue notifications totalled 1,295 with 568 confirmed; 1 death confirmed and another under investigation; dengue incidence 70.5 per 100,000 (autochthonous). Chikungunya: 121 notifications, 115 confirmations; no deaths; incidence 7.8 per 100,000. Zika: 8 notifications, 3 confirmed; incidence 0.4. Vector control: 574,889 properties inspected; 60,826 treated; 68,063 water deposits treated; 17,104 risk deposits eliminated. Health Secretary Lúcia Helena Barboza Sampaio urges continued prevention and community participation. Dengue vaccination with Qdenga is free via SUS for ages 10–14 (two doses). Seek care for fever, body pains, headache, rash, or intense joint pain.

article.articleHeadline: Dead monkey had yellow fever; City Hall reinforces prevention measures.
article.articleSummary: Uberlândia, in Minas Gerais’ Triângulo Mineiro, Brazil, confirmed a dead monkey tested positive for yellow fever, with laboratory confirmation by Fundação Ezequiel Dias (Funed). The SES/MG implemented preventive measures, including active vaccination outreach to unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated people and intensified yellow fever vaccination campaigns. Monkeys are natural sentinels signaling viral presence but do not transmit to humans; residents should report abnormal or dead monkeys to authorities. Vaccination is free via SUS, and has been part of Minas Gerais’ immunization program since 2008; since 2017 the schedule uses a lifelong single dose, with a booster for those who received the first dose before age five. Severe yellow fever can present with high fever, jaundice, hemorrhages, and sometimes multi-organ failure, with a 20–50% fatality rate in severe cases. As of 12 July 2026, authorities emphasize rapid, responsible prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Yogyakarta Special Region Finds 25 Leprosy Cases, Active Screening Now Strengthened.
article.articleSummary: Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) in the Yogyakarta Special Region (DIY), Indonesia, reached 25 diagnosed cases through the second quarter of 2026. The DIY provincial government is strengthening active screening, surveillance, and community education to accelerate elimination, aiming to detect cases earlier, shorten treatment initiation, and reduce transmission and stigma. The move follows a National Leprosy Conference 2026 in Jakarta on 10 July 2026, where the Deputy Governor and the DIY Health Office reaffirmed commitments and called for expanded case finding at Puskesmas and hospitals, enhanced laboratory capacity, and public communication strategies with Kominfo DIY. Initial symptoms can be subtle, including white or red patches and numbness, often delaying care. Health authorities emphasize early treatment—free at public facilities—and warn that earlier detection prevents disabilities and curbs spread.

article.articleHeadline: 30,000 people in Bali have been bitten by animals suspected of rabies since winter.
article.articleSummary: Rabies concerns surged in Bali, Indonesia, where from January–May 2026 almost 30,000 people were bitten by animals suspected of rabies and about 21,000 received emergency post-exposure vaccination; five rabies deaths were recorded in the first five months of 2026, following 16 fatalities in 2025. Experts note rabies is not restricted to dogs; other mammals such as cats, bats, and monkeys can transmit the virus. The spate of attacks raises health‑risk questions about the consumption of dog or cat meat, a cultural issue in parts of Indonesia including Bali, North Sumatra, and Sulawesi. Islamic law prohibits canid meat, but Indonesia lacks a unified national ban; several localities prohibit dog meat. Bali banned dog‑meat sales in 2023, with penalties up to 50 million rupiah (about $2,800) or three months’ imprisonment.

article.articleHeadline: Health Minister Inspects Rongjia Ya Leprosy Comprehensive Zone, Strengthens Coordinated Efforts in Leprosy Prevention and Control.
article.articleSummary: On 12 July 2026, Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin visited the Rongjia Leprosy Comprehensive Zone in Barambaru village, Tomarat District, Makassar, to strengthen coordinated leprosy prevention and control. Accompanied by Makassar Deputy Mayor Aliyah Mustika Ilham, he held direct discussions with leprosy survivors, including Mohammad Ali, who are undergoing treatment. He emphasized that leprosy is a bacterial disease that is curable with medication, and that patients are no longer contagious after starting therapy; early detection is essential to prevent disability. The minister also stressed the need to combat stigma against recovered individuals to facilitate social reintegration. Deputy Mayor Ilham welcomed the visit, noting it brings hope to residents and former patients (OYPMK). The visit aims to bolster collaboration among the central government, WHO Indonesia, the Sasakawa Health Foundation, and partner organizations to accelerate leprosy elimination and foster a more inclusive society.

article.articleHeadline: 5 Ways HIV Is Transmitted You Must Know: Don't Misunderstand the Facts.
article.articleSummary: HIV is transmitted through the exchange of virus-containing body fluids, not via ordinary social contact. The article outlines five transmission routes, highlighting two key risks in Samarinda and Balikpapan, East Kalimantan: (1) unprotected sexual intercourse, where virus in semen or vaginal fluids can infect partners, especially with genital injuries or untreated sexually transmitted infections, and (2) shared use of needles for drugs, tattoos, piercings, or other needle-based procedures without proper sterilization. It notes ongoing concern in Samarinda, where the health office reported 184 new HIV cases through May 2026, with Balikpapan mentioned in related reporting. Prevention emphasizes correct and consistent condom use and regular health checkups to reduce transmission and curb stigma against people living with HIV. The piece stresses accurate understanding of transmission routes to guide prevention without increasing discrimination.

article.articleHeadline: Parents should be vigilant for several characteristic signs of pediatric TB.
article.articleSummary: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) in Indonesia may present without the classic adult symptom of a persistent cough. Dr. Madeleine Ramadhani Jasin Sp.A, Subsp Respi (K), of the Unit Kerja Koordinasi Respirologi under the Indonesian Pediatric Society (IDAI), notes that weight loss or stagnation for two to three months—even with improved nutrition—is a key sign of TB in children. The article emphasizes that children often do not exhibit coughing, which can delay diagnosis. Reported by ANTARA and linked to Indonesia’s IDAI respiratory network, the guidance underscores vigilant recognition of TB in the pediatric population. As of July 12, 2026, awareness among Indonesia’s pediatric health community remains essential to early detection and treatment of pediatric TB presentations.

article.articleHeadline: Expert Advice on Addressing the Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) Threat at Former Natural Disaster Sites.
article.articleSummary: On 12 July 2026, researchers from Universitas Negeri Padang evaluated the former flood site in Kelurahan Tabing Banda Gadang, Nanggalo, Padang, West Sumatra, for dengue risk after the flash flood (pascagalodo). Environmental changes have created standing water and poorly managed water storage, boosting Aedes aegypti breeding and the threat of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF/DBD). The team promotes community-led prevention, especially empowering PKK women as Jumantik larval monitors to check jentik at home. Health expert Elsa Yuniarti stresses early recognition of DBD symptoms and prompt care, alongside household measures: clean drains, covered and routinely emptied water containers, and removal of water-holding items. Prevention centers on 3M Plus—drain, close, recycle—plus weekly larval checks and ovitrap monitoring. Ongoing recovery requires government–community collaboration and sustained household education to curb DHF risk.

article.articleHeadline: GHS confirms no Cholera outbreak after floods, urges continued preventive measures
article.articleSummary: Ghana Health Service confirms no cholera outbreak after the June floods; as of 11 July 2026 no cholera cases have been registered. Flood conditions—heaps of refuse, blocked drains, and stagnant water—trigger preventive measures rather than outbreaks. A disinfection campaign is underway in flood-affected communities following a nationwide clean-up (July 10–11, 2026) to eliminate disease-causing organisms and reduce cholera, typhoid, and other sanitation-related illnesses. Disinfection has occurred at Tema Station Market and Adabraka Polyclinic, with Korle Klottey Municipal Assembly and sanitation partner LCB Worldwide collaborating as part of broader post-flood interventions. Dr. Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, Director-General, stresses prevention over reaction, noting treatment is costly. Authorities urge continued sanitation, hygiene, and vigilance; after cleaning, further disinfection and fumigation are planned to prevent outbreaks in the affected areas of Ghana.

article.articleHeadline: What is the brain-eating amoeba, and what causes it? In which countries is the brain-eating amoeba present? Is the brain-eating amoeba found in the sea, or does it occur in saltwater?
article.articleSummary: Naegleria fowleri, the brain-eating amoeba, caused the death of 11-year-old Jordan Smelski during a Costa Rica vacation, reviving attention to PAM (Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis). The organism enters via the nose and inflames brain tissue; it is not transmitted by drinking water. Symptoms typically appear 1–12 days after exposure and include severe headache, fever, nausea, neck stiffness, photophobia, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, and coma; progression is rapid and most patients die within days. Risk factors include swimming in warm freshwater lakes, natural hot springs, spa water, poorly chlorinated pools, and high-nose-water exposure during water sports. It is not person-to-person and not from food or drinking water. Historically common in warm climates: US, Pakistan, Australia, India, Thailand, Mexico, Costa Rica, with newer reports in Slovakia, Italy, Belgium, Taiwan, and Minnesota. As of 2026-07-12, Kerala, India reports hundreds of cases; saltwater cannot sustain the amoeba; seas pose lower risk.
